description: We've been building stuff together since Grade 10 at Old Scona, and now we're second-year EE co-ops at UAlberta doing it at hackathons. I'm Akileash. I've never needed a complicated answer for what I enjoy: it's building things. Right now that's a buck converter for ARVP's sub. I'm Harsit. I basically built Jarvis for drones, and I run a tech YouTube channel with 3k+ subs. Last time we teamed up, we made glasses that turn ASL into speech.
summary: Marcia is a Mars spacewalk planner and helmet display built on real NASA data. In Plan mode, a crew in the habitat picks science stops in Jezero Crater, and Marcia routes the safest walk there and back over a 1 m HiRISE terrain model, steering around steep slopes, soft sand, low-thermal-inertia ground and crew-drawn avoid zones. A turn-back ring shows how far the crew can go and still get home on the oxygen left after the reserve, and flags any stop beyond it. In Walk mode, the same route moves to a helmet HUD with heading, oxygen and return margin, alerts for going off route, steep slopes and low oxygen, and one-tap Replan from where the astronaut stands. Marcia also checks NASA's live DONKI space-weather feed and blocks or tightens a walk during solar storms. One click exports a mission brief listing the route, margins, alerts, every dataset used, and which numbers are estimates. The same pipeline runs a second site at Gale Crater, showing the method works beyond one location.
details:
What does it do?

Marcia is like Google Maps for a Marswalk. An astronaut or mission planner picks the science stops they want at Jezero or Gale Crater, sets their oxygen supply, reserve and max slope, and Marcia plans the safest out-and-back route from the habitat. It then guides the walk on a helmet-style HUD.

How does it work?

- Terrain: the USGS Mars 2020 TRN HiRISE DTM mosaic (1 m) becomes a 3 km × 3 km walking-cost grid of 5 m cells. Gale uses HiRISE DTM DTEEC_019698_1750_019988_1750_U01 through the same pipeline. Slopes over the limit (25° by default) are blocked.

- Sand and soft ground: sand comes from the Stack et al. (2020) Jezero geologic map, and soft ground from Mars Odyssey THEMIS thermal inertia (Edwards & Buz 2021). The route avoids both.

- Science: MRO CRISM minerals (Parente et al. 2021) and geology layers show what each stop is worth. Jezero stops are real Perseverance sampling sites, and Gale stops are Curiosity sites, each with the rover's own photos.

- Oxygen: a turn-back ring shows how far you can go and still get home with your reserve left (480 min with a 20% reserve by default, walking at 50 m per minute). Stops outside it are flagged before you leave.

- Space weather: Marcia checks live NASA DONKI data. A solar energetic particle (SEP) event in the last 24 h, or a CME predicted to reach Mars within 12 h, takes the walk from planned to blocked. An M- or X-class flare tightens it, raising the reserve from 20% to 30%.

- Walk mode: the HUD shows oxygen margin, hazard alerts and the next stop's photo. Replan reroutes from where you stand.

- Mission brief: one click gives a share link and a PDF with the route, margins, alerts, every dataset used, and which numbers are estimates.

What are the benefits and impact?

Tools like Mars Trek show Mars data layers, but they don't plan a walk. Marcia puts safety and science on one map, so an explorer can see the safest route and the best science together and make a go/no-go call before leaving the habitat. A four-stop Jezero route is planned in about 50 ms in any browser, so students, analog teams and the public can plan a real Marswalk with real NASA data today.

What tools did you use?

TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet, CesiumJS (3D terrain view), Zustand, Tailwind CSS, and Vitest (374 automated tests). Terrain and imagery were processed with GDAL and QGIS. Hosted on GitHub Pages at trymarcia.work, deployed with GitHub Actions.

How is it creative?

- Google Maps for Mars: route planning on real NASA terrain, open to anyone in a browser.

- Oxygen as a map: the turn-back ring turns a life-support budget into a boundary you can see.

- Live DONKI space weather turned into a go/no-go call for the EVA.

- One pipeline, any HiRISE site: Gale was added with the same code as Jezero.

What factors did we consider?

Astronaut safety (slope, sand, soft ground, oxygen reserve, solar storms); real NASA data, with every source cited in our README; being clear about what's measured and what's modelled (surface weather, oxygen use and walking speed are estimates, and Gale has no sand layer, so it runs slope-only and says so); colour-blind-safe palettes; and keeping the app working if a live feed is down.

Links

Live app: https://trymarcia.work/

30-second video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YVANA9DpVXE

Use of AI

We used AI tools (Claude, Claude Code and Cursor) for research, brainstorming, coding, debugging and editing. Our team designed the system, chose the data and safety rules, and reviewed and tested every change. All data and images are real NASA or published scientific data, not AI-generated. No NASA logos, insignia or mission identifiers were used; the Marcia logo is our own.
